info.title: PanelAlpha Engine API
info.description:
REST API for managing projects, domains, databases, files, and server
infrastructure in the PanelAlpha hosting platform.

**A "project" is what earlier versions of this API called a "user":** one
hosting account with its own container, domains, databases and files. The
resource is documented here under `/projects`.

Every `/projects/...` path below is also served at the identical
`/users/...` path, with the same parameters, body and response. That alias
is deprecated but permanent -- it is not scheduled for removal, so existing
integrations do not need to change. New clients should use `/projects`.

Note that `mysql/users` and `app/users` are *not* the renamed resource:
they are MySQL accounts and accounts inside the deployed application
respectively, and keep their names.

post.summary: File a bug report about a deployed application
post.description: Sends a bug report to PanelAlpha through the same telemetry channel the install events use: the report is queued in the local spool and delivered by the next `telemetry:ship` run, so a 201 means "accepted and queued", not "delivered". The response carries the exact redacted report that will be transmitted, so a caller can show it before or after filing. A report is always about one `project`, and the engine gathers the evidence itself rather than asking anyone to paste it: `app.inspect` is the same report GET /projects/{username}/inspect answers with (what the engine detects the application to be, what it would build, which ports it would publish, and the drift between that and what the last deploy froze); `app.health` is a live probe of every published port from inside the account container, with the checks that ask whether what answered is the application at all; `deploy` is what the last deploy decided; `log_tail` is the end of its deploy log at telemetry tier 2. The health probe is the only part that costs seconds and touches the container — turn it off with `attach_health: false`. Everything gathered is redacted before it leaves: tokens, credentials, email addresses, public IPs and home directory paths are masked wherever they appear, and any value under a key naming a secret is replaced outright. `contact` is the one exception and the one field that identifies a person: it is sent exactly as given, is never filled in automatically, and is omitted entirely when not supplied. Requires telemetry to be enabled (`TELEMETRY_ENABLED`, `TELEMETRY_BUG_REPORTS`) and a monitoring host to be configured; otherwise the call fails rather than dropping the report.

title.description: One-line headline. Reports are grouped across installs by this plus `area`, so write the symptom rather than the incident: numbers, paths and ids inside it are normalised away before grouping.

post.description: A deny rule is placed above every allow rule, so it wins; an allow rule goes last. An inbound deny covers the host's ports and the ports Docker publishes (scope both, as a fail2ban ban does) unless scope published is asked for. A rule needs a port, a source or a destination. A rule that matches the same traffic as one already there, whatever its action or comment, is refused naming that rule, which is left as it is. Do not open a port for an application: sites are reached through the engine's webserver.

scope.description: Default host: the host's own ports. published: ports Docker publishes; port and destination are the container's, and direction is in. Neither scope reaches the other. An inbound deny sent without a scope is both; a scope that is sent is kept, except both on an outbound rule, which is host.

direction.description: Default in. both: traffic from source coming in and to source going out, as one rule; needs source and no destination.

A comment that starts with by Fail2Ban, which marks the bans fail2ban makes, is refused.

post.summary: Create a vault slot for a secret that will be pasted in a browser
post.description: Mints a paste slot. Returns `ref` (`vault:<key>`, pass it whole where the secret would go -- e.g. the `git_token` field of project_create) and `url` (the form the customer opens and pastes the secret into, open for `url_expires_in` seconds). The secret expires only if `expires_in` is given; it is then refused and deleted automatically. **The secret never passes through the API caller** -- that is this mechanism's whole purpose, for agents that must not relay a private-repository token through a conversation. `scope` decides where it may be used: `project` (the default) belongs to the first project it is given to and is refused everywhere else; `global` may be used by any project that names it. Nothing uses a secret unasked. Give `purpose` so the entry can be recognised later: the secret is never readable again, so the listing is all you have. **A pasted secret is final** -- to replace one, delete it and create a new link. The form checks a `git_token` or `cloudflare_api_token` before saving it, with the same calls the engine makes when it uses one: a git token against `verify_with.repo_url` (required for the check), a Cloudflare token for its account and Tunnel access, plus the zone of `verify_with.hostname` when given. A refused token is not stored and the link stays open. `verification` on status then says whether it was checked.

type.description: The request field the reference will be passed in (e.g. `git_token`, `env_vars`). Free-form snake_case -- the field the caller will send `vault:<key>` in. The paste form shows help from `resources/vault/<type>.md` when that file exists, else the default help.

scope.description: `project` (the default): usable by one project only -- the first one it is given to claims it, and any other project is refused. `global`: usable by any project that names it. Either way it is used only where a request passes its `vault:<key>`, and there may be any number of each type.

expires_in.description: Seconds until the secret expires. After that it is refused and deleted, with no one having to remove it. Omitted, it never expires. A project that already used the secret keeps the copy it stored.

project.description: Only with `scope: project`: the project that owns the secret from the start, so only that project can read it. The project need not exist yet. Omitted, the first project that reads the secret owns it.

purpose.description: What this secret is for, in your words -- "deploy key for the shop repo", "Cloudflare token for the staging zone". Shown on the paste form, so the person handing over a credential can see why, and returned by `list`. Several entries share one `type`, and the secret can never be read back, so this is what tells them apart later when deciding which to delete.
purpose.example: Deploy key for the shop repo

verify_with.description: What the pasted secret is checked against before it is saved. `git_token`: `repo_url`, the HTTPS repository the token must be able to read. `cloudflare_api_token`: `hostname` (optional), a domain whose zone the token must see. A refused token is not stored and the form asks again; an unreachable host saves it unchecked.

post.summary: Generate an SSH deploy key in the vault
post.description: Generates an ed25519 key pair and keeps it in the vault, so a project can be created with an SSH remote in one call. The answer carries `public_key`: add that line to the repository as a read-only deploy key (GitHub: Settings > Deploy keys), then pass `ref` (`vault:<key>`) as `source.auth.key` with `source.auth.type: deploy_key` on POST /projects or PUT /projects/{username}/source. The private half is never returned. The host keys of github.com, gitlab.com and bitbucket.org ship with the engine; for any other git server pass `host` (`git.example.com` or `git.example.com:2222`) and its SSH host keys are read now and trusted from then on. `scope` works as for every vault secret: a `project` key (the default) belongs to the first project created with it, a `global` one may be used by any project that names it. The key is stored on the project that uses it, so deleting the vault entry later does not take it away from that project.

post.summary: Inspect an application source and report its stack, ports and services
post.description: Detects what an application is without deploying it. The source may be a Git repository URL or the username of an existing project (its files under the account home directory); a directory on this server is refused. A Git source is cloned shallow without file contents, and only the files detection reads are fetched; a public github.com repository that git refuses is read from its file list instead, and one that cannot be read either way (submodules, a manifest over 1 MB) is cloned shallow in full. Each goes into a temporary directory that is removed again, and `source.method` says which (`partial`, `tree` or `clone`). `application.verdict` is what a deploy would serve: `deployable`; `no_start_command`, which deploys but whose package.json says nothing about starting a server; `placeholder`, only the "Project not configured" page; or `not_deployable`. `application.deployable` is false for the last two, with the reason in `application.issue`; a port nothing names is `ports.issue`. Each is a finding (`code`, `message`, its facts) with the `hints` that act on it. Values from .env files are never returned - only the variable names. A project username returns the same report as GET /projects/{username}/inspect, including the `deployment` snapshot its last deploy froze and the `drift` between that and the files on disk - so a caller that already has a username does not need the other endpoint. A token limited to some projects may name only those as a project source.

source.description: Repository URL (the scheme may be left out), or the username of an existing project.

type.description: How to read `source`. Detected from its shape when omitted. `path` is not accepted: inspecting an arbitrary server directory is not exposed over the API.

subdirectory.description: Inspect this directory inside the source instead of its root. For a project the source root is the account home directory, so this is a path under /home/<username> such as "project/apps/api" or "public_html".

git_token.description: Access token for a private HTTPS repository. A `vault:<key>` of a `global` vault entry is accepted here in place of the literal token. A `project` entry is accepted while no project owns it yet, and inspecting does not assign it; one a project owns is refused. Omitted, the clone is anonymous.

recipe.description: Preview the deploy this recipe would produce instead of the one detection picks. Takes an id from `application.candidates` in a previous inspection, and is the same field the deploy endpoints accept - so what this previews is what deploying with it executes. An id this engine does not ship comes back as `application.issue` rather than an error.

stages.description: Preview a deploy that overrides stages: the same `stages` payload the deploy endpoints take, reported here without deploying anything. A stage named replaces that stage in the returned plan; one left out keeps the platform defaults. Each command in `application.stages` says where it came from in `source`: manifest, app_config or request.

get.summary: Inspect a project's deployed application files

Reads /home/<username>/project by default (the main domain's document root for the classic PHP templates); `subdirectory` selects another directory under the account home. Values from .env files are never returned - only the variable names. This is POST /source/inspect with `type: project`, addressed by username: same report, same field names, and readable with a GET. The older spellings - the `/source-inspection` path and the `path` parameter - still work and are deprecated.

post.summary: List the branches and tags of a remote Git repository
post.description: Reads a remote with `git ls-remote --symref`, without cloning it or touching any account, so a branch picker can be shown before a project exists. Runs globally, not for one project. `branches` is the default branch first, then by name; `tags` is by name. `default_branch` is the branch HEAD pointed at, or null when the remote named none. A public repository needs no token; a private one takes a `git_token` (a `vault:<key>` is accepted in its place). A repository URL whose host resolves to an internal address, or does not resolve at all, is refused 422 with `problems[{field: repository, code: host_refused}]`.

repository.description: Repository URL. The scheme may be left out; the host is not guessed for owner/repo shorthand.

git_token.description: Access token for a private HTTPS repository. A `vault:<key>` of a global vault entry is accepted in place of the literal token; a project entry is accepted while no project owns it, and listing does not assign it. Omitted, the remote is read anonymously.

get.summary: List the projects allowed to use the Engine API
get.description: One entry per allowed project: the scope its token was minted with, whether the token may call MCP tools too, when it was allowed and its token id. The tokens themselves are never returned. Only container projects receive the API address, the token and the certificate in their environment; a classic project is allowed and reachable, and gets nothing in its container. Refused with 403 for a token scoped to some projects: it is not a project route.

403.description: The caller's token is scoped to some projects

get.x-mcp-description: Lists the projects allowed to call this engine's API, with the scope of each token. Refused 403 for a project-scoped token.

put.summary: Allow a project to use the Engine API, or change its scope
put.description: Mints a token for the project with the abilities the scope implies, lets the project's containers reach the API port, and queues an apply that delivers the API address, the token and, where a client needs one, the certificate to the running application without a rebuild. Allowing a project that already carries this scope and this `mcp` flag changes nothing at all; a changed scope or flag replaces the token, and the old one is revoked once the new one is in use. `scope` is `self` (only this project), `all` (every project on this engine), or a list of existing project usernames; an unknown one is refused with 422. Only a container project may be allowed: a classic project has no container to receive the environment, so it is refused with 422 and the code api_access_container_only. Refused with 403 for a token scoped to some projects. To replace a token without changing the scope, use POST /system/api-access/{project}/rotate.

scope.description: What the token may act on. `self`, `all`, or a list of existing project usernames.

mcp.description: Whether the token may also call MCP tools.

403.description: The caller's token is scoped to some projects

422.description: A scope that is neither self, all, nor a list of existing projects; mcp, not a boolean; or a project that is not a container project

put.x-mcp-description: Allows a project to call this engine's API, minting a token limited to the given scope (self, all, or a list of existing projects) and opening the host firewall to the project's containers. Allowing a project that already carries that scope changes nothing. A classic (PHP hosting) project is refused. Refused 403 for a project-scoped token.

post.description: Create the Deploy Hook for a git-connected checkout, so a push to its tracked branch redeploys the project. Optional `path` defaults to `project` on DinD and the document root of the main domain on FPM/LiteSpeed (`project` is the Deploy-managed checkout). Returns the `url` to register in the git host and the `secret` to sign with. The secret is shown ONCE, in this response, and can never be read again: store it now, or rotate later. Asking again returns the same hook (200) without the secret and never rotates it. On the Deploy-managed checkout every push to the tracked branch force-updates it to match the repository (local changes to tracked files and untracked files that are not engine-managed are discarded before the rebuild) and the response carries a `warning` saying so. On a Site Git checkout (e.g. `public_html`) a push only fast-forwards, with no build: untracked files such as uploads are left alone, and when git refuses because of a local change, an untracked file at an incoming path or rewritten history, nothing changes and the delivery's result is `pull_refused`. The response's `tls` block says whether the engine's certificate is one a git host trusts outright (`state: valid`) or self-signed (`state: self_signed`); when self-signed it carries `instructions`, one paragraph per supported provider (github, gitlab, bitbucket-cloud, bitbucket-data-center) on making that provider call the hook anyway. Optional `provider` on the request narrows `instructions` to that one provider. `tls.warning` is set when the engine has no public address, so a git host on the internet could not reach the hook at all. 422 when the checkout is not connected to git. With `register: true` the engine also creates the webhook at the git provider the checkout came from, using the token the checkout itself clones with, and the response carries `registration` (`provider_hook_id` and `registered_at`; a GitLab hook made before 2.2 cannot be signed, and `registration_warning` then says to rotate it); the token needs permission to manage repository webhooks (GitHub Webhooks read and write on a fine-grained token or admin:repo_hook on a classic one, GitLab maintainer, Bitbucket admin), else 422 `provider_token_missing` or `provider_permission_denied`; a provider that cannot be reached is 502. The provider API is called only at a public address of the repository's host, pinned to the address checked, and a redirect is followed only on that same host; any other host is never called and the answer is 422 `host_refused`. The Engine hook is created either way, and `registration: null` with `registration_warning` says when the engine has no provider API for that host. When this call created the hook and the registration is then refused, the refusal carries the hook as a 201 would have answered it, `secret` included, in `problems[0].hook` (422) or `hook` (502): it is the only time that secret is shown.

Nested names such as `api.<name>.panelalpha.online` are not available: an application that needs them needs a domain of the customer's own plus addon domains. Labels are first come, first served across the fleet, so a name in use is refused; deleting the tunnel releases it again. `cloudflare` puts a CNAME in a zone the project's own API token controls, so it fits a custom domain; set the token first with PUT /projects/{username}/settings/cloudflare-api-token. The hostname's zone is looked up before the project's tunnel is created or started. A token Cloudflare does not accept answers 422 `cloudflare_token_invalid`; one missing a permission answers 422 `cloudflare_permission_denied` naming it (Account · Cloudflare Tunnel · Edit, Zone · Zone · Read or Zone · DNS · Edit); any other refusal 422 `cloudflare_request_refused` with Cloudflare's message; a rate limit 503 `cloudflare_rate_limited` and an outage 502 `cloudflare_unavailable`, both worth retrying later. Omit `hostname` with the `panelalpha` provider and the engine allocates a free `preview-<8 random [a-z0-9]>` label under panelalpha.online; it draws a new label when one is taken, and answers 409 `tunnel_hostname_unavailable` when five labels in a row are. `purpose` separates a long-lived address (`default`) from one a preview opens (`preview`); `ttl_minutes` gives either a lifetime the engine enforces -- returned as `valid_until`, and stored under `details.expires_at` -- 24 hours for a `preview` tunnel that does not name one. The proxy's own `details.valid_until` is a separate value the engine does not act on. An expired tunnel is removed by the engine and never returned by GET.

post.description: Creates a project and deploys it in the background: answers 202 with a task. Poll GET /tasks/{id} until it is completed, failed or cancelled; the deploy log is teed into its task logs (GET /tasks/{id}/logs, or the stream), and GET /projects/{username}/deploy-log keeps timings and history. **The body is typed.** `source` says where the code comes from, and its `type` decides what else it takes (schema ProjectSource): `none` an empty project (a container one waits for files), `git` a repository (HTTPS, with an optional token; or an SSH remote with a deploy key from POST /vault/deploy-keys), `archive` a .zip/.tar.gz from POST /uploads or a URL, `project` a copy of another project, `wordpress` a php_hosting project with WordPress installed. `runtime` is `container` or `php_hosting`; a source implies its own (git and archive: container, wordpress: php_hosting, project: the original's), omitted it is container, and a contradicting one is refused. Limits, hosting settings, dedicated addresses and build options sit in objects of their own. A key the body does not have is refused (`unknown_field`), and a field of the flat body (`git_repo`, `template`, `memory_limit`, ...) with `legacy_field` and its `replacement`; every refusal names the field as sent (`source.url`, `limits.memory`, `domain.name`), with the same codes the flat body answers. post.description: Accepts the source site URL and how to reach it, stores the secret (wp-admin password or plugin token) encrypted on the migration record, and queues the migration job. method wp_admin (default) logs into the source wp-admin with username and password and installs the migrator plugin there; login_url names a custom login page. method manual_plugin takes no credentials: the user installs the plugin from POST /wordpress/migrations/plugin-package and source_token is its token. source_ip reaches the source at that public address with its own Host, e.g. while its DNS already points elsewhere. Check the same body first with POST /wordpress/migrations/test and pass the `domain` it answers: without `domain` a start takes it from `url`, and once the job has found the site's real home it moves to that home's domain (without www.) when it differs and is free, and fails when it is taken. Returns 202 with the record id and status pending. The response never includes the password or migrator token. The migration runs asynchronously in a chain of bounded queue jobs and can take from minutes to several hours on a large site. Poll the get endpoint every 1-2 minutes until status is completed, failed or cancelled; do not start a second migration for the same site while this one is running. The site keeps its own domain: a new empty classic project is created on it with no tunnel (or the existing `project` is used), the source sends the transfer to this engine's IPv4 whatever the domain's DNS says, and with PanelAlpha Connect a preview tunnel shows the site until the DNS points here. Then the engine issues the certificate and removes the preview by itself. Every call to the source plugin's transfer routes carries the import's own token. A transfer already running on the source that this engine did not start is never taken over: remote_sync fails naming it, and a resume after it has finished goes on. An engine whose default IPv4 is not public, and not mapped to a public address in the IPv4 NAT map, answers 409 engine_address_private and stores nothing, since the source could not send the transfer to it; EGRESS_ALLOW_PRIVATE lifts that for a source on the same private network.

get.description: Returns the migration steps and log. Never includes the password or migrator token. Status is pending, running, completed, failed, cancelling or cancelled. stale is true while a pending or running migration has not reported for 15 minutes: resume it. A step is only marked completed when it finishes, so a long step such as migrate_files can stay pending for a long time while the migration is still working: this is normal, keep polling. Treat the migration as failed only when status is failed (the failing step and message are in step_log). progress names the current step (step, step_index of step_count) and gives percent over the whole run, weighted setup 0-10, database 10-40, files 40-95 and finish 95-100; phase_percent is how far the current phase is. While the database or files transfer, item is the table or file being sent and message counts the chunks. updated_at is the run's heartbeat: a stale one while status is running means the run has stalled. warnings lists what the import noticed and went on with: plugin_unauthenticated means the source plugin is older than 1.2.0 and answers its transfer routes without a token, so anyone can copy the site while it is installed; the engine removes it (wp_admin), or the user must (manual_plugin, see notices), as soon as the import ends, fails or is cancelled.

post.summary: Resume a failed or stalled WordPress migration
post.description: Re-queues a migration that is in status failed, or that is running or pending but stale (no heartbeat in progress.updated_at for 15 minutes, e.g. its worker died), and continues from the step that did not complete. Steps are safe to repeat: the project the import created is adopted, WordPress core and its database are not created twice. A wp_admin migration that failed after its plugin reached the source has had the plugin removed there; resume installs it again and restarts the transfer. Rejects any other status with 409, including a running migration that is still reporting: wait for it. A migration that has had no activity for 7 days loses its stored password and tokens (step_log says secrets_expired): resume it with password (wp_admin) or source_token (manual_plugin) again, otherwise 422. A transfer it left unfinished then starts again from install_destination_plugin.

password.description: wp_admin: the wp-admin password, required once it was cleared; replaces the stored one. Never returned.

target_domain.description: The domain the imported site answers on; null until a panelalpha.online name is allocated for an IP source.

preview_url.description: panelalpha.online preview of the site while its domain still points elsewhere; null without Connect and once the domain points here.

422.description: The cleared password or source_token was not sent

post.summary: Cancel a WordPress migration and remove what it made
post.description: Sets status cancelling and queues the cancel; a running migration stops between steps and batches. The cancel stops the transfer on the source (manual_plugin), removes the migrator plugin from the source (wp_admin only: a manual_plugin source keeps the plugin the user installed), deletes the project the import created, or removes the imported files and database from an existing `project`, removes the preview tunnel and clears the stored password and tokens. It ends as cancelled. What could not be done on the source is noted in step_log; anything left on this engine keeps the migration cancelling, and cancelling it again retries. Allowed for pending, running, failed and cancelling migrations; 409 for completed or cancelled ones.
